disclaimer: Ekseem Maar Net is a family passion project, made with love for our brother. It is not a medical app. Everything here is general, surface-level information from public guidelines and research. It is not medical advice. Eczema is different for everyone, so always speak to a doctor, dermatologist or pharmacist before you start, stop or change any treatment.

categories.title: Main Contributing Factors
categories.subtitle: What matters most, in order
categories.intro: Eczema comes from a leaky skin barrier and an immune system that overreacts. It often runs in families, and food is rarely the cause. What helps most is moisturising every day, treating flares early and avoiding everyday irritants.

items.name: Weak skin barrier
items.note: Eczema skin loses water and lets irritants and germs in. Moisturising every day is the most important habit.

items.name: Under-treated flares
items.note: Lots of people are scared of steroid creams and wait too long. Treating a flare early with the right cream settles it faster.

items.name: Genes and family history
items.note: About 70% of people with eczema have a family member with eczema, asthma or hay fever. It's nobody's fault.

items.name: Over-reactive immune system
items.note: Allergy-type messengers in the body (IL-4, IL-13, IL-31) cause the redness and itch. The newest medicines block exactly these.

items.name: Staph bacteria
items.note: A common skin germ that grows well on eczema patches and makes flares worse. Treating the eczema keeps it down.

items.name: The itch-scratch cycle
items.note: Scratching damages the skin, which makes it itch more. Habit reversal (see Treatment) helps you break the cycle.

items.name: Soaps, bubble bath and detergents
items.note: Anything that foams strips the skin barrier. Use a soap-free wash instead.

items.name: Fragrance and perfume
items.note: Found in lots of creams, washes and washing powder. It's a common irritant and allergen.

items.name: Stress
items.note: Stress makes the itch worse, and eczema itself is stressful. Ways to cope and support from others help (see Motivation).

items.name: Heat and sweat
items.note: Stay cool, rinse sweat off and moisturise. No need to stop sport or play.

items.name: Tobacco smoke
items.note: Second-hand smoke makes eczema worse. Keep your home and car smoke-free.

sections.title: What about food
sections.intro: Every major guideline says don't cut out foods "just in case". In one clinic, 19% of children on elimination diets developed new allergies, some of them severe. Only remove a food if a doctor confirms an allergy.

items.name: Oats, wheat and gluten
items.note: No benefit in avoiding them, unless you've been diagnosed with coeliac disease or a wheat allergy.

items.name: Milk, cheese and butter
items.note: Fine unless a cow's milk allergy is diagnosed. Don't cut out dairy without a dietitian, because kids need the calcium.

items.name: Yoghurt, amasi and maas
items.note: In South African toddlers, fermented milk was linked to less eczema.

items.name: Eggs
items.note: Eggs aren't dairy. Egg allergy is common in South African kids with eczema, but only avoid eggs if an allergy is proven.

items.name: Nuts and peanuts
items.note: They don't cause eczema if you're not allergic. Giving smooth peanut early (from 4–6 months) prevents peanut allergy. Whole nuts are a choking risk under 5.

items.name: Refined sugar
items.note: Sugar has no histamine, and a study found it doesn't cause flares. Still limit it for your teeth and general health.

categories.title: Wonder Cures
categories.subtitle: Newer treatments for moderate to severe eczema
categories.intro: None of these cure eczema, but for moderate–severe eczema they can give long-lasting clear skin. They're prescription medicines a dermatologist chooses, and you still moisturise every day alongside them. This page is just so you know what's out there. Ask your dermatologist if any of them suits you.

items.name: Dupixent (dupilumab), injection
items.note: A biologic injection every 2–4 weeks that blocks the IL-4/IL-13 allergy pathway. Registered in South Africa from 6 years (from 6 months in the US and EU). The main side effect is eye irritation. No routine blood tests needed.

items.name: Rinvoq (upadacitinib), daily tablet
items.note: A JAK inhibitor tablet that works fast and did very well in trials. Registered in South Africa from 12 years. It has a boxed warning (infections, clots, heart events, cancer) and you need blood tests. No grapefruit.

items.name: Cibinqo (abrocitinib), daily tablet
items.note: A JAK inhibitor, registered in South Africa in April 2025 (from 12 years in the EU). It has the same JAK safety warnings and blood test checks as Rinvoq.

sections.title: Approved overseas, ask your dermatologist
sections.intro: Approved in the US or EU, but we couldn't confirm South African registration when we checked.

items.name: Ebglyss (lebrikizumab), injection
items.note: An IL-13 biologic, given monthly once you're on the maintenance dose. From 12 years. The most common side effect is conjunctivitis (pink eye).

items.name: Adtralza / Adbry (tralokinumab), injection
items.note: Another IL-13 biologic. Approved from 12 years in the US.

items.name: Nemluvio (nemolizumab), injection
items.note: Blocks the itch signal (IL-31), so the itch eases quickly. From 12 years.

items.name: Olumiant (baricitinib), tablet
items.note: A JAK inhibitor approved for eczema in the EU from 2 years. The same JAK warnings apply.

items.name: Opzelura (ruxolitinib cream)
items.note: The first JAK cream, approved in the US from 2 years (Sept 2025). Only for short-term use on small areas.

items.name: Zoryve (roflumilast cream)
items.note: A non-steroid cream you use once a day. Approved in the US from 2 years (Oct 2025).

items.name: Vtama (tapinarof cream)
items.note: A non-steroid cream you use once a day. Approved in the US from 2 years. About 9% of people get folliculitis (inflamed hair follicles).

items.name: Anzupgo (delgocitinib cream)
items.note: For adults with chronic hand eczema (US approval, July 2025).

items.name: Amlitelimab
items.note: A new kind of injection (OX40 ligand) that might only be needed every 12 weeks. Phase 3 results are mixed, and applications for approval are expected in late 2026.

items.name: Rocatinlimab
items.note: Trials were stopped in March 2026 after safety concerns came up.

categories.title: Treatment
categories.subtitle: What doctors recommend, step by step
categories.intro: All the big guidelines (AAD, NICE, European and South African) use the same steps. Moisturise every day, treat flares early with the right-strength anti-inflammatory cream, then use it twice a week to keep flares away. Used correctly, steroid creams are safe and they work.

sections.title: The steps
sections.intro:
1. Every day, even when the skin is clear, put fragrance-free moisturiser on the whole body.
2. At the first sign of a flare, put a steroid cream of the right strength on the red patches (a mild one on the face).
3. On the face, eyelids and skin folds, a steroid-free cream like tacrolimus may suit better.
4. Once the skin calms down, keep using the cream twice a week on the usual spots so flares don't come back.
5. If it's still not under control, ask about light therapy, tablets or injections (see Wonder Cures).

items.name: Moisturisers (emollients)
items.note: The base of all eczema care. Use them on the whole body every day. Kids need about 250–500 g a week. The best one is the one you'll actually use.

items.name: Fragrance-free products
items.note: Fragrance is one of the most common skin allergens. Pick products without perfume or dyes.

items.name: Petroleum jelly (Vaseline)
items.note: Cheap, works well and has no fragrance. South African guidance recommends it when money is tight.

items.name: Aqueous cream as a moisturiser
items.note: Left on the skin, it damages the barrier. Only use it as a soap substitute and rinse it off.

items.name: Topical corticosteroids (steroid creams)
items.note: First choice for any flare, mild or severe, at the right strength for that part of the body. A big 2024 review found no extra skin thinning with short-term use.

items.name: Fingertip unit (FTU)
items.note: A line of cream from the tip of an adult's finger to the first crease, about 0.5 g. That covers two adult palms. Put it on red patches only, once or twice a day.

items.name: Twice-weekly maintenance
items.note: Once a flare settles, put the cream on the usual spots twice a week. This prevents new flares.

items.name: Tacrolimus / pimecrolimus
items.note: Steroid-free creams that work well on the face, eyelids and skin folds. Any burning settles after a few days. Big studies show no real cancer risk.

items.name: Newer non-steroid creams
items.note: Ruxolitinib, roflumilast and tapinarof creams are approved overseas but not yet confirmed in South Africa. See Wonder Cures.

items.name: Topical steroid withdrawal (TSW)
items.note: Doctors recognise it, but it isn't well understood yet. It's mostly linked to long-term misuse of strong steroids on the face or genitals. Follow your doctor's plan instead of stopping suddenly.

items.name: Habit reversal
items.note: When you feel the urge to scratch, clench your fists or press on the spot for 30 seconds instead. Small trials show it helps.

items.name: Keep nails short
items.note: Short nails do less damage when you scratch, especially at night. Cotton mittens help for babies.

items.name: Be gentle
items.note: Short lukewarm baths, pat dry and don't scrub.

items.name: Soft, loose cotton clothing
items.note: A big trial found silk is no better than cotton. Loose, soft clothes that breathe are what matter.

items.name: "Just stop scratching"
items.note: That rarely works on its own. Get the itch under control with treatment and try habit reversal instead.

items.name: Written eczema action plan
items.note: Ask your doctor for one. The Allergy Foundation of South Africa has a template you can use.

items.name: Phototherapy (narrowband UVB)
items.note: Medical light treatment at a dermatologist, for eczema over large areas. Not the same as sunbathing or sunbeds.

items.name: Ciclosporin
items.note: A fast-acting tablet for severe eczema. Short-term only, with kidney and blood pressure checks. Avoid grapefruit.

items.name: Methotrexate
items.note: Works well but needs regular blood tests. Keep alcohol to a minimum. It isn't registered for eczema in South Africa, so doctors use it off-label.

items.name: Oral steroids (prednisone, cortisone)
items.note: Guidelines say don't use them, and are even firmer about this for kids. They cause rebound flares and side effects. Only as a short rescue by a specialist.

items.name: Non-drowsy antihistamines
items.note: A big review found they don't reliably help eczema itch. They're useful for hay fever or hives.

items.name: Drowsy antihistamine at night
items.note: Only a short 7–14 day trial during a flare that's ruining sleep, and only on a doctor's advice. Never use promethazine (Phenergan) under 2 years.

items.name: Coal tar
items.note: An old treatment with weak evidence. It stains, smells and makes skin sensitive to the sun. Only use it if a specialist advises it.

items.name: Dust-mite covers
items.note: For most people they don't reliably help. They might only help if you have a proven dust-mite allergy.

items.name: Food elimination diets
items.note: Only cut out a food if a doctor confirms an allergy. Avoid internet and high-street allergy tests.

items.name: Tea tree oil in the bath
items.note: It's a common skin allergen and can make eczema worse.

sections.title: See a doctor the same day if…
sections.intro:
• Eczema suddenly gets worse, weeps, crusts over or has yellow spots (it could be infected).
• There are painful, punched-out blisters or sores, especially with a fever. This could be eczema herpeticum, which is a medical emergency.
• A baby's eczema is severe or isn't settling.

categories.title: Remedies
categories.subtitle: Home and natural remedies, and which ones are worth trying
categories.intro: Natural doesn't always mean gentle, and some popular remedies are common skin allergens. Use these with your prescribed treatment, never instead of it. Try anything new on a small patch of skin for a few days first.

items.name: Vaseline (petroleum jelly)
items.note: Cheap, fragrance-free and it works. South African guidelines recommend it.

items.name: Virgin coconut oil
items.note: Did better than mineral oil in a trial with kids who had mild to moderate eczema, and may cut down staph bacteria. Don't use it on infected skin.

items.name: Sunflower seed oil
items.note: Helped protect the skin barrier in a study. A good natural oil to use.

items.name: Colloidal oatmeal
items.note: Eases the itch for a while. Pick fragrance-free products, and stop if it stings.

items.name: Wet wraps after a bath
items.note: Really helps with bad flares for a short time, with a doctor or nurse guiding you. Never use them on infected skin.

items.name: Shop-bought ointments and creams
items.note: Plain fragrance-free moisturisers are fine. Stay away from unlabelled or imported "eczema creams", because some have hidden steroids in them.

sections.title: Unproven, so try with care
sections.intro: There are no good eczema trials for these. Lots of people use them without trouble, but stop if your skin reacts.

items.name: Aloe vera gel
items.note: No trials of aloe on its own. Many gels have alcohol or fragrance in them, and some people have had allergies to it.

items.name: Shea butter
items.note: A decent plain moisturiser if your skin is fine with it. No eczema trials.

items.name: Cassia alata
items.note: Only shown to fight bacteria in the lab. No studies on people with eczema.

items.name: Castor oil
items.note: No eczema trials, and some people have had skin allergies to it.

items.name: Black seed oil (Nigella sativa)
items.note: Only one small trial, and some people have had severe allergic skin reactions. Never put it on undiluted. Taking it by mouth is unproven.

items.name: Speensalf (udder cream)
items.note: A teat ointment made for dairy cows, not for eczema, and what's in it varies. Use a fragrance-free moisturiser instead.

items.name: Calendula and chamomile
items.note: These are in the daisy family, and people with eczema are more often allergic to them.

items.name: Honey / manuka
items.note: Only one tiny study with no comparison group. Never give honey to babies under 1.

items.name: Hemp / CBD creams
items.note: Only one small trial. Products vary a lot and aren't regulated.

items.name: Rooibos on the skin
items.note: Looks promising, but only in mouse studies so far.

items.name: Tea tree oil
items.note: A well-known skin allergen, and worse from old bottles. It can make your eczema flare.

items.name: Turmeric on the skin
items.note: A proven skin allergen, and it stains too. Eating it in food is fine.

items.name: Apple cider vinegar
items.note: A study found it didn't help the skin barrier and irritated most people's skin.

items.name: Olive oil
items.note: Damaged the skin barrier in a study. Don't use it for baby massage either.

items.name: Milk of magnesia
items.note: No evidence. It's alkaline, and eczema skin does better with slightly acidic products.

items.name: Worcestershire sauce
items.note: No evidence. The vinegar and spices sting and irritate broken skin.

items.name: Witch hazel
items.note: No eczema evidence, and lots of products have drying alcohol in them.

categories.title: Supplements
categories.subtitle: What the research says about vitamins, pills and products
categories.intro: Most supplements haven't been shown to help eczema. Only vitamin D (if your levels are low or in winter) and short-term melatonin for sleep have a bit of support. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about everything you take.

items.name: Vitamin D
items.note: Helped a little in trials, mostly in people with low levels or in winter. Ask for a blood test, and don't take huge doses.

items.name: Melatonin
items.note: Helped kids with eczema fall asleep about 21 minutes faster. Short-term only, at a dose your doctor gives.

items.name: Vitamin B12 cream (on the skin)
items.note: Small trials against a dummy cream showed it helped. B12 liquid by mouth has no evidence unless you're low in B12.

sections.title: No proven benefit
sections.intro: Probably fine at normal doses, but probably not worth the money for eczema.

items.name: Probiotics
items.note: Probably make little or no difference to eczema, going by a big review of 39 trials.

items.name: Omega-3 / fish oil
items.note: Reviews found no real benefit. Eating oily fish is still good for you.

items.name: Vitamin C
items.note: No proven benefit, but no sign it harms eczema either. Strong skin serums may sting.

items.name: Vitamin E
items.note: Reviews found no benefit.

items.name: Zinc & copper
items.note: Might help only if you're really low in them. There are no studies on copper.

items.name: Calcium & magnesium
items.note: No eczema trials found.

items.name: Milk thistle
items.note: No evidence that it eases itch.

items.name: L-lysine, chlorophyll, quercetin, collagen
items.note: No eczema trials found.

items.name: Evening primrose & borage oil
items.note: Worked no better than a dummy pill across 27 trials.

items.name: "Liver detox" supplements
items.note: Detoxing your liver has no link to eczema. Some herbal mixes have caused liver damage.

items.name: Non-drowsy antihistamines for eczema itch
items.note: Don't reliably help eczema. Only useful for hay fever or hives.

items.name: Phenergan (promethazine) every night
items.note: Not for routine use. Never give it to children under 2 years, as it can stop their breathing, and tablets are not for under 5s. Only for short use in a flare, on prescription.

items.name: Prednisone / cortisone tablets
items.note: Not a supplement. These are prescription steroids, and guidelines advise against them for eczema because the eczema flares up again when you stop (rebound flares).

items.name: Retinol skin products
items.note: Dries out and irritates eczema skin. Don't use it in pregnancy.

items.name: Fragrance & perfumes
items.note: One of the most common skin allergens. Pick unperfumed products.

categories.title: Causes & Triggers
categories.subtitle: Why eczema happens and what sets off flares
categories.intro: Eczema comes from your genes, a weak skin barrier and an immune system that over-reacts. Triggers then set off flares, and they're different for everyone. A simple flare diary helps you spot your own pattern.

items.name: Genes and family history
items.note: Eczema runs in families where there's eczema, asthma or hay fever.

items.name: Skin barrier (filaggrin)
items.note: Some people's skin is missing strong building blocks like filaggrin, so water gets out and irritants get in.

items.name: Immune system
items.note: The immune system over-reacts, a bit like an allergy, and that causes redness and itch.

sections.title: Irritants
sections.intro: These are hard on anyone's skin, and on eczema skin most of all.

items.name: Soaps, detergents, bubble baths
items.note: Use a soap-free wash and skip anything that foams.

items.name: Perfumes and fragrance
items.note: Irritates the skin and is also a common allergen. Pick fragrance-free creams, washes and washing powder.

items.name: Scratchy or rough fabrics
items.note: Coarse wool and tight, hot clothes make you itch. Soft, loose cotton is best.

items.name: Tobacco smoke
items.note: Second-hand smoke is a known trigger. Keep your home and car smoke-free.

items.name: Paraffin, coal and wood smoke, traffic fumes
items.note: South African studies link these to more eczema. Let plenty of fresh air in when you burn fuel indoors.

items.name: Reactions to creams
items.note: If your eczema was under control and suddenly gets worse after a new product, ask about patch testing for a contact allergy.

items.name: Heat and sweat
items.note: Keep cool and don't overdress babies. Rinse off sweat and moisturise, but don't stop exercising.

items.name: Dry air and cold
items.note: Highveld winters dry the skin out, so moisturise more often when it's dry or cold.

items.name: House dust mites
items.note: Only matters if you're allergic. Mite-proofing doesn't help most people much, so don't buy pricey products just in case.

items.name: Pollen
items.note: Matters if you're allergic, often with seasonal flares or flares around the eyes. Ask about testing.

items.name: Pet fur and dander
items.note: Only avoid pets if an allergy is proven. Contact with dogs early in life is linked to less eczema.

items.name: Damp and mould
items.note: May make allergies worse. Fix damp for your general health, though the evidence for eczema itself is limited.

items.name: Hard water
items.note: Water softeners didn't help eczema in a big trial. Metro water in South Africa is mostly soft anyway.

items.name: Stress, including family or relationship stress
items.note: Stress makes the itch worse, and eczema adds stress. It works both ways, so support and ways of coping help.

items.name: Hormones
items.note: Some women flare in the week before their period or during pregnancy. Plan extra skin care for those times.

items.name: Staph infection
items.note: Weeping, crusting or yellow spots can mean infection. See a doctor.

items.name: Eczema herpeticum (emergency)
items.note: Painful clusters of blisters or punched-out sores, often with a fever. Get medical help the same day.

items.name: Yeast (Malassezia)
items.note: In some teens and adults, eczema on the head and neck may get better with antifungal treatment.

items.name: Baby with gut symptoms
items.note: If a baby has eczema plus vomiting, colic, diarrhoea or poor growth, ask your doctor about food allergy.

items.name: "Gut health" / leaky gut
items.note: Gut bacteria may be different with eczema, but probiotics don't reliably help and "leaky gut" isn't a recognised diagnosis.

items.name: Candida
items.note: No good evidence that thrush in the gut causes eczema, or that anti-candida diets help.

items.name: Liver, spleen, "detox"
items.note: Liver or spleen problems don't cause eczema. Some herbal cleanses can harm the liver or have hidden steroids in them.

items.name: Gluten
items.note: Not a common eczema trigger. Guidelines say don't go gluten-free unless you've been diagnosed with coeliac disease or a wheat allergy.

items.name: A healthy diet can cure eczema
items.note: Not true. Eating well is great for your general health, but no diet cures eczema, and cutting out foods can cause new allergies.

items.name: Eczema heals naturally
items.note: Not always. Many kids get better as they grow, but not all, and flares often come back. Untreated eczema is bad for sleep and skin. Herbal "natural cures" are unproven.

items.name: Eczema is contagious
items.note: Not true. You can't catch eczema. Infected patches can spread germs though, so keep them treated and wash hands.

items.name: Only children get eczema
items.note: Not true. It can start at any age, and there's a second peak in older adults.

items.name: Steroid creams always thin the skin
items.note: Not true. Thinning is rare when you use them as directed, even with twice-weekly use to prevent flares.

items.name: Children with eczema shouldn't be vaccinated
items.note: Not true. Vaccinate on schedule. Only some strong eczema tablets affect live vaccines, so ask your doctor.

categories.title: Drinks & Beverages
categories.subtitle: What's fine to drink, and what to keep for treats
categories.intro: No drink has been proven to cure or calm eczema, and very few need to be avoided. Keep your skin hydrated from the outside with moisturiser. Pick drinks that are good for your sleep and general health.

items.name: Water
items.note: The best everyday drink. It won't moisturise your skin on its own. Moisturiser does that.

items.name: Rooibos
items.note: Caffeine-free and fine for the whole family. Lab studies look interesting, but there's no proof yet that it calms eczema in people.

items.name: Green tea
items.note: Fine to drink. The skin benefits in studies came mostly from creams, not cups of tea. Has caffeine.

items.name: Oolong tea
items.note: One small 2001 study, without a control group, hinted at a benefit. Not proven, but fine if you enjoy it.

items.name: Black tea
items.note: No evidence it makes eczema worse. Has caffeine, so not for babies and young children.

items.name: Cow's milk
items.note: Only cut it out if a doctor confirms a milk allergy. Cutting it for no reason can hurt nutrition and may even raise allergy risk.

items.name: Plant milks (soya, oat, almond)
items.note: From age 1, pick unsweetened, calcium-fortified ones. No rice drinks for under-5s.

items.name: Coconut milk drink
items.note: No link to eczema either way. Not a full milk replacement for kids, so check with a dietitian.

items.name: Kefir and probiotic drinks
items.note: Fine as food, but a big review found no proof that probiotics treat eczema.

items.name: Bone broth
items.note: Fine as food, but there's no evidence it helps eczema.

items.name: Coffee
items.note: No proven link to eczema. Skip it later in the day, because bad sleep makes itch worse. Not for children.

items.name: Matcha
items.note: Fine for adults, but high in caffeine. Skip it late in the day and don't give it to kids.

items.name: Fruit juice (apple, grape, citrus)
items.note: No effect on eczema, but sugary. For young kids, mix 1 part juice with 10 parts water and give it with meals. Citrus can redden the skin around a toddler's mouth.

items.name: Vegetable juice (beet, celery)
items.note: No proven benefit. Some people are allergic to celery, and handling lots of it in the sun can cause a skin reaction.

items.name: Smoothies
items.note: Fine. For kids, dilute it and give it with meals. Leave out any food that's a confirmed allergy.

items.name: Kombucha
items.note: No proof it helps in people. It's acidic, often sugary and can have a little alcohol in it. Adults only.

items.name: Soda and fizzy drinks
items.note: No direct link to eczema, but bad for teeth and general health. Not for young children.

items.name: Energy drinks (under 18)
items.note: Linked to short, poor sleep and other harms in young people. Adults should keep them occasional.

items.name: Grapefruit juice on certain medicines
items.note: Don't drink it if you take ciclosporin or upadacitinib (Rinvoq), because it raises the medicine levels in your blood. Check every medicine leaflet.

sections.title: Alcohol
sections.intro: There's no strong proof that alcohol causes flares. It can make your skin flush and itch, and it messes with sleep, which makes itch worse. People notice red wine, beer and darker spirits most, because they have more histamine, sulphites or congeners. If you drink, keep it light and have water in between.

items.name: Gin, vodka, silver (blanco) tequila
items.note: Clear spirits have the fewest congeners. Use plain mixers like soda water, and stop a few hours before bed.

items.name: Red wine
items.note: The alcohol most often blamed for itch and flushing, because of its histamine and sulphites.

items.name: White and sparkling wine
items.note: Less histamine than red, but it still has sulphites.

items.name: Beer and cider
items.note: Fermented, so they contain biogenic amines (histamine-type compounds). Some people notice flushing or itch.

items.name: Brandy, whisky, dark rum
items.note: Darker spirits have more congeners and are linked to worse hangovers. Keep them for now and then.

items.name: Sake and rice wines
items.note: Fermented like wine and beer, so not a clear spirit. Treat sake like wine.

items.name: Cocktails, alcopops, liqueurs
items.note: Lots of sugar and mixed ingredients, so it's hard to tell what sets you off. No grapefruit cocktails if you're on ciclosporin or Rinvoq.

items.name: Under 18, pregnant or breastfeeding
items.note: Don't drink alcohol at all. Drinking while pregnant is linked to eczema in the child.

items.name: On methotrexate or ciclosporin
items.note: Keep alcohol to a minimum, because methotrexate and alcohol both strain the liver. Ask your doctor or pharmacist.

categories.title: Food
categories.subtitle: No special diet needed, just eat well
categories.intro: There's no special eczema diet. Eat a varied, balanced diet and only cut out a food if a doctor or allergist confirms an allergy. If you have to cut out a main food like milk, get a dietitian to help. Treat the skin first.

items.name: Oily fish (pilchards, snoek, sardines, mackerel)
items.note: Healthy fats. Eating fish in a baby's first year is linked to less eczema. Fish-oil capsules don't treat eczema though.

items.name: Amasi, maas and plain yoghurt
items.note: A South African study linked fermented milk to less eczema in toddlers. Fine unless you're allergic to milk.

items.name: Vegetables and fruit
items.note: Butternut, sweet potato, pumpkin, spinach and morogo are all great. No evidence they make eczema worse.

items.name: Mediterranean-style eating
items.note: Legumes, whole grains, olive or canola oil and nuts. One study linked it to milder eczema, and it's good for your overall health.

items.name: Lean meat, chicken, beans and lentils
items.note: Good for protein and iron.

sections.title: Babies: start allergens early
sections.intro: Giving babies smooth peanut and well-cooked egg early, from about 4–6 months, lowers the chance of allergy. In the LEAP trial, peanut allergy dropped from 13.7% to 1.9%. If your baby has severe eczema, talk to your doctor first.

items.name: Well-cooked egg (from about 4–6 months)
items.note: Giving it early and regularly lowers the risk of egg allergy.

items.name: Smooth peanut butter (from about 4–6 months)
items.note: Thin it with water or breast milk. Never give whole nuts to under-5s, because they can choke on them.

items.name: Mother avoiding foods while pregnant or breastfeeding
items.note: Not recommended, unless the baby has a proven allergy and a doctor advises it.

items.name: Mielie pap, samp, rice
items.note: No evidence that maize makes eczema worse. Add vegetables and protein.

items.name: Bread, wheat and gluten
items.note: Going gluten-free doesn't help unless you've been diagnosed with coeliac disease or a wheat allergy.

items.name: Oats (eating)
items.note: Eating oats is fine. Oat creams on broken skin may make some babies sensitive to oats.

items.name: Milk, cheese and butter
items.note: Fine unless a cow's milk allergy is diagnosed. Kids need the calcium.

items.name: Eggs
items.note: Eat them as normal unless an egg allergy is proven. Eggs aren't dairy.

items.name: Nuts and peanuts
items.note: They don't cause eczema if you're not allergic.

items.name: Soya
items.note: Fine unless you're allergic. Soya formula only on medical advice, and not before 6 months.

items.name: Sugar and sweets
items.note: Doesn't cause eczema (sugar has no histamine), but limit it for teeth and weight.

items.name: Fast food and takeaways
items.note: Surveys link fast food 3 or more times a week to more severe eczema.

items.name: Boerewors, polony, viennas
items.note: Salty and fatty, and a South African study linked fried meats to allergy. Enjoy them now and then.

items.name: Biltong and droëwors
items.note: No link to eczema either way. Very salty, so don't overdo it.

items.name: Citrus, tomato, strawberries (messy eaters)
items.note: The juice can redden the skin around the mouth. That's usually irritation, not allergy. Put on a barrier ointment before meals.

sections.title: Avoid only if a doctor confirms an allergy
sections.intro: A food allergy usually shows within 2 hours, with hives, swelling, vomiting or wheezing. A positive skin or blood test on its own doesn't prove an allergy. Internet and IgG "intolerance" tests are no use.

items.name: Cow's milk (confirmed allergy)
items.note: The most common allergen in babies. Only use special formula on medical advice, and retest after 6–12 months.

items.name: Egg (confirmed allergy)
items.note: Common in South African kids with eczema. Many outgrow it, so recheck after 1–2 years.

items.name: Peanut and tree nuts (confirmed allergy)
items.note: Can cause severe reactions. If you're allergic, carry an emergency plan.

items.name: Wheat, soya, fish, shellfish (confirmed allergy)
items.note: Known allergens. Only avoid them after proper testing.

items.name: Elimination diets "just in case"
items.note: Little benefit, and a real risk of poor growth and new, sometimes severe, allergies.

items.name: Low-histamine, low-nickel, anti-candida, detox diets
items.note: Not proven for eczema, and you risk poor nutrition.

items.name: IgG food "intolerance" tests
items.note: No evidence they're any use. They lead to cutting out foods for no reason.

categories.title: Water & Bathing
categories.subtitle: Baths, showers, swimming and wet wraps
categories.intro: How you bathe matters more than how often. A recent trial of 438 people found daily and weekly bathing worked equally well. Use lukewarm water, keep it short, skip the soap and moisturise straight after.

sections.title: Everyday bath or shower (soak and seal)
sections.intro:
1. Lukewarm water (test it with your wrist), 5–10 minutes.
2. Wash with an emollient (moisturiser) or a soap-free wash. Don't scrub.
3. Pat dry with a soft towel and leave the skin a bit damp.
4. Within about 3 minutes, put prescribed cream on the eczema patches and moisturiser everywhere else.
5. Put on loose cotton clothes.

items.name: Bath or shower, as often as suits you
items.note: Daily or a few times a week both work. What matters is moisturising straight after.

items.name: Lukewarm water, 5–10 minutes
items.note: Hot water and long soaks make the itch worse.

items.name: Moisturise within 3 minutes
items.note: Locks the water in while your skin is still damp.

items.name: Emollient instead of soap
items.note: Normal soap, bubble bath and shower gel strip the skin. Don't use aqueous cream either, because it irritates.

items.name: Pat dry, don't rub
items.note: Use a clean, soft towel. Don't share towels while a flare is infected.

items.name: Hot showers and long baths
items.note: Heat sets off itch and dries out the skin.

items.name: Bubble bath, scented gels, soap
items.note: The fragrance and detergents irritate eczema skin.

items.name: Dilute bleach bath (moderate–severe eczema)
items.note: A review of 10 trials found it probably makes eczema milder. Only with your doctor's OK, usually 2–3 times a week. See the recipe below.

items.name: Colloidal oatmeal
items.note: May soothe some people. Stop if it stings, because some people are sensitive to oats.

items.name: Dead Sea salt
items.note: One small study found better skin hydration. Can sting broken skin. Optional, not a treatment.

items.name: Epsom salt or baking soda
items.note: No real evidence for eczema, and it may sting. Optional.

items.name: Rooibos in the bath
items.note: Only looks promising in mouse studies. Harmless to try, but stop if it irritates.

items.name: Emollient bath oils
items.note: A big trial found no benefit on top of normal moisturising, and they make the bath slippery. Rather spend the money on a leave-on moisturiser.

items.name: Vinegar soaks
items.note: No benefit, and most people in testing got irritated skin.

items.name: Tea tree oil in the bath
items.note: A common skin allergen, and old bottles are worse. Risky on broken eczema skin.

sections.title: Bleach bath recipe (South Africa)
sections.intro:
Only if your doctor recommends it. You're aiming for about 0.005% bleach.

Jik is about 3.5% (check your bottle and use the plain, unscented one). So you need 1.4 mL of bleach per litre of water:
• Baby bath (~15 L): about 21 mL (1 tablespoon + 1 teaspoon)
• Half bath (~80 L): about 115 mL (just under ½ cup)
• Full bath (~150 L): about 215 mL

US recipes use stronger 6% bleach, so don't copy their cup measures. Mix the bleach into lukewarm water before you get in. Soak for 5–10 minutes and keep the water away from your eyes. Pat dry and moisturise straight away. Never mix bleach with other cleaners.

items.name: Water softener
items.note: A big trial found it didn't help eczema, even in very hard water. Johannesburg and Cape Town water is soft anyway.

items.name: Shower filter
items.note: No studies show it helps eczema, so it's not worth buying for that.

items.name: Borehole water
items.note: Can be much harder than municipal water. A lab hardness test is cheap if you're curious, but softeners still haven't been shown to help.

items.name: Swimming pool (chlorine)
items.note: Most people with eczema can swim. Moisturise before, then shower and moisturise straight after.

items.name: Sea swimming
items.note: Fine if it feels OK, but it may sting cracked skin. Rinse off in fresh water and moisturise afterwards.

items.name: Sunscreen outdoors
items.note: If other sunscreens sting, use a fragrance-free mineral one (zinc or titanium).

sections.title: Wet wraps (for flares)
sections.intro:
Ask a doctor or nurse to show you first. Never wrap infected eczema (weeping, crusting or yellow spots).
1. Bath, pat dry, and put on prescribed cream and moisturiser.
2. Wet a cotton layer in warm water and wring it out so it's damp, not dripping.
3. Put it on, with a dry layer and loose pyjamas over the top.
4. Leave it on for 2 hours or overnight, then moisturise again.
5. Use it for about 7–14 days, then check back with your doctor.

items.name: Wet wrap therapy
items.note: Calms bad flares and helps with sleep. Short-term only, because more steroid gets absorbed through the skin.

items.name: Stay hydrated
items.note: Good for your general health, but drinking extra water won't fix dry eczema skin. Moisturiser will.

categories.title: Clothing & Laundry
categories.subtitle: What to wear and how to wash it so skin stays calm
categories.intro: Go for loose, soft clothes that let the skin breathe. No fabric treats eczema. Even special silk clothing made no difference in a trial with 300 children. The wrong fabrics, finishes and detergents can make the itch worse though.

items.name: 100% cotton
items.note: Soft and cool, and it soaks up sweat. Check the label, because "cotton-rich" can be mostly polyester.

items.name: Superfine merino (17.5 micron or finer)
items.note: Did better than cotton in two small trials, both paid for by the wool industry. Try one base layer first.

items.name: Bamboo viscose and TENCEL (lyocell)
items.note: Soft and smooth, and it soaks up sweat. Kind to eczema skin, but there are no trials on it.

items.name: Silk, including "eczema" silk garments
items.note: Fine if you like how it feels, but a big trial found it doesn't treat eczema. Spend the money on moisturiser first.

items.name: Wicking sportswear
items.note: Well-fitting sports synthetics are fine for exercise. Cotton, bamboo or merino might still feel gentler.

items.name: Polyester and synthetics (everyday)
items.note: For lots of people they trap heat and sweat, which sets off the itch.

items.name: Lace, sequins, denim, fake fur
items.note: These often irritate. Fine over a soft layer, just not right on the eczema.

items.name: Coarse wool next to the skin (jerseys, blankets)
items.note: The thick fibres prick and itch. Wear wool over a cotton layer instead of right against the skin.

items.name: Loose fit
items.note: Tight clothes rub and trap heat. Buy a size up for uniforms and workwear.

items.name: Cut out labels
items.note: Snip them off close to the seam, or buy tagless.

items.name: Rough seams
items.note: Wear it inside-out, or tape over seams that bother the skin.

items.name: "Non-iron" and "wrinkle-free" finishes
items.note: Often treated with formaldehyde resins, a known clothing allergen.

items.name: Dark or bleeding dyes
items.note: Disperse dyes are some of the most common textile allergens. A rash in the body folds is worth a patch test.

items.name: Nickel jeans studs and belt buckles
items.note: A rash under the stud at your belly button can point to a nickel allergy. Cover the stud with fabric tape and ask for a patch test.

items.name: Wash new clothes before wearing
items.note: Gets rid of extra dye and finishing chemicals. Do the same with school uniforms and bedding.

items.name: Fragrance-free detergent
items.note: Look for "fragrance-free". "Unscented" can still have perfume in it to mask smells.

items.name: Use less detergent and add an extra rinse
items.note: Too much detergent leaves residue in the fabric. Try this before you switch brands.

items.name: Bio or non-bio
items.note: Either is fine. Big studies found the enzymes don't irritate skin or cause allergies.

items.name: Fabric softener
items.note: Some people are fine with it and some aren't. Only use fragrance-free, and test it on its own.

items.name: Change one product at a time
items.note: Give each change a month. Detergent often gets the blame for flares it didn't cause.

items.name: Monthly hot empty wash
items.note: Run the machine empty at 90 °C once a month to clear emollient build-up and bacteria.

items.name: Cotton gloves or mittens at night
items.note: Less damage from scratching in your sleep. For kids, all-in-one sleepsuits with mitts help.

items.name: Breathable sleepwear and cotton sheets
items.note: Use light layers you can take off, and keep the room cool (16–18 °C).

items.name: Spiky roller balls
items.note: No proof they help, and they might damage broken skin. Try pressing, pinching or a cold pack instead.

items.name: Fire safety
items.note: Clothes and bedding soaked in emollient catch fire easily. No smoking in bed or candles near it, and wash bedding often.

items.name: Sun-protective clothing and a hat
items.note: UPF clothing means you need less sunscreen on sensitive skin.

items.name: Sport kit
items.note: Wear breathable layers you can take off. Wash kit after every session and shower soon after.

items.name: School uniforms
items.note: Buy them loose, cut out the tags and wash before wearing. Add a cotton layer underneath.

categories.title: Health
categories.subtitle: Skin care, sleep, exercise, infections and more
categories.intro: Eczema affects more than the skin. Sleep, mood, eyes and allergies can all be part of it. These everyday habits and warning signs help you stay well all round.

sections.title: See a doctor today if…
sections.intro:
• Eczema suddenly gets painful, with clusters of blisters or small punched-out sores, often with a fever. This could be eczema herpeticum, which is an emergency. If it's near the eyes, you need an eye doctor too.
• The skin is weeping, has pus or yellow crusts, gets worse fast, or there's a fever. This could be a bacterial infection.
Emergency numbers: 10177 (ambulance) · 112 (from a cellphone).

items.name: Moisturise every day, even when clear
items.note: At least twice a day, ideally 3–4 times. Adults with eczema all over can go through about 500 g a week.

items.name: Soak and seal
items.note: Short lukewarm wash, pat dry, medicine on the red patches, then moisturiser everywhere else within 3 minutes.

items.name: Smooth on, don't rub
items.note: Go in the direction the hair grows. Rubbing heats up the skin.

items.name: Use a spoon or pump
items.note: Keep fingers out of the tub. Replace opened tubs after an infection.

items.name: Short, smooth nails
items.note: Check them every week. If scratching happens anyway, it does less damage.

items.name: Cool emollient from the fridge
items.note: Feels soothing on itchy skin. Never warm emollients in the microwave.

items.name: Cool bedroom (16–18 °C)
items.note: Heat makes night itch worse. Use a fan in summer and light layers you can adjust.

items.name: Thick moisturiser before bed
items.note: Put it on well before lights out so you don't overheat.

items.name: Regular bedtime, screens off an hour before
items.note: Normal good sleep habits help with eczema too. Avoid caffeine and alcohol late at night.

items.name: Melatonin
items.note: Helped kids fall asleep faster, but only helped the skin a little. Ask a doctor or pharmacist first.

items.name: Regularly losing sleep
items.note: A sign the eczema isn't under control. Go back to the doctor, because treatment can be stepped up.

items.name: Regular exercise
items.note: Lowers stress and helps sleep and mood. Don't skip sport because of eczema.

items.name: Plan for sweat
items.note: Dress in layers, take breaks and drink cool water. Shower and moisturise soon after.

items.name: Sit out when skin is infected or raw
items.note: Resting protects the broken skin.

items.name: Enjoy the sun, but don't burn
items.note: Some people get better in the sun and others flare. Never try to tan or burn. Stay in the shade from 11:00 to 15:00.

items.name: Mineral sunscreen SPF30+
items.note: Fragrance-free zinc oxide or titanium dioxide is often gentler. Test a new one on a small patch for 3–5 days.

items.name: Medical light therapy
items.note: Narrowband UVB at a dermatologist is a real treatment. Sunbathing isn't the same thing.

items.name: Highveld winter
items.note: Very dry air and heaters. Moisturise more often with a thicker cream, keep showers lukewarm and don't sit close to the heater.

items.name: Coastal humidity and heat waves
items.note: Sweat and heat set off the itch. Use lighter creams in the day, wear loose cotton and have a cool shower.

items.name: Smog and veld-fire days
items.note: Pollution is linked to flares. Stay inside when you can and rinse your skin afterwards.

items.name: Load-shedding
items.note: Keep a battery fan, a cold pack in a cooler box and a pump bottle of moisturiser next to the bed.

items.name: Routine vaccines
items.note: Eczema is no reason to skip or delay vaccines, and neither are steroid creams.

items.name: Live vaccines on Dupixent or JAK tablets
items.note: Don't have live vaccines (e.g. MMR, yellow fever) during treatment. Catch up on vaccines before starting, and plan travel vaccines with the specialist.

items.name: Old smallpox vaccine (ACAM2000)
items.note: Not for people with eczema or anyone they live with. The newer mpox vaccine (JYNNEOS) is fine.

items.name: Asthma, hay fever, itchy eyes
items.note: Part of the same "atopic" family. Each one needs its own treatment.

items.name: Food allergy (mainly children)
items.note: Linked to early, severe eczema. Don't cut out foods without a doctor (see Food).

items.name: Low mood and anxiety
items.note: Common and treatable, and not a weakness. Support numbers are on the Motivation page.

items.name: Don't rub your eyes
items.note: Eczema and eye rubbing each roughly triple the risk of keratoconus (thinning of the cornea). See an optometrist if your vision goes blurry.

items.name: Sore or red eyes on Dupixent
items.note: A common side effect, usually mild. Tell your doctor early, because eye drops usually help.

items.name: Bone, heart and weight
items.note: There are small links in adults. Keep up the usual health checks with your GP.

items.name: Written eczema action plan
items.note: Green is daily care, amber is what to do in a flare, red is call the doctor. Ask your doctor to fill one in.

items.name: Weekly POEM score
items.note: Seven questions about the past week, scored 0–28 (0–2 clear, 3–7 mild, 8–16 moderate, 17–24 severe, 25–28 very severe).

items.name: Weekly photos
items.note: Same spots, same light. Write down itch and sleep too, because redness is harder to see on darker skin.

items.name: Who to see
items.note: Pharmacist for mild patches. GP if treatment isn't working or sleep is disturbed. Dermatologist for frequent flares or if a contact allergy is suspected.

categories.title: Motivation & Affirmations
categories.subtitle: For the person living with eczema, and the people who love him
categories.intro: Eczema wears you down in ways other people don't always see. Bad nights, constant itch, people staring, and the creams every single day. Feeling low is common and it can be treated. Eczema treatments today are also better than ever.

sections.title: Need to talk? (South Africa)
sections.intro: If anyone talks about not wanting to live, call one of these numbers together. Don't wait.

items.name: SADAG Suicide Crisis Helpline
items.note: Free, open 24 hours.

items.name: Cipla Mental Health Helpline
items.note: Open 24 hours. You can also SMS 31393 or WhatsApp 076 882 2775 (8am–5pm).

items.name: Adcock Ingram Depression & Anxiety Helpline
items.note: Open 8am–8pm.

items.name: Dr Reddy's Mental Health Helpline
items.note: Open 8am–8pm.

items.name: Emergency (life in danger)
items.note: Ambulance 10177 · from a cellphone 112.

sections.title: Daily affirmations
sections.intro: Pick one for today. Say it, write it down, or stick it on the mirror.

items.name: My skin is one part of me, not the whole of me.
I can have a hard skin day and still have a good day.
A flare is like bad weather. It doesn't last forever.
Itchy moments pass. I have ways to get through them.
I've lived with this for years, and that makes me strong.
Looking after my skin is a way of looking after me.
Today I'll do what I can, and that's enough.
I am more than the itch.
Bad nights don't cancel good days.
How my skin looks doesn't decide what I'm worth.
I don't owe anyone an explanation for my skin.
I'm allowed to rest when my body is tired.
Asking for help is a skill, and I'm getting better at it.
I can be patient with my skin and with myself.
Every time I stick to my routine, that's a win.
I'm learning what my body needs, one week at a time.
People who love me want to help, and I can let them.
I can feel frustrated and still be hopeful.
Today I'll be gentle with myself.
My routine doesn't have to be perfect. I just keep coming back to it.
I can speak up to my doctor. My experience matters.
I'm proud of how I keep showing up.
I'm allowed to say no to advice that doesn't help me.
My family is on my team.
I can take this one hour at a time.
I can still enjoy things on itchy days.
Progress isn't a straight line, and that's okay.
There are more good treatments than ever
items.note: Since 2023, guidelines strongly recommend lots of new injections, tablets and creams. Ask a dermatologist what suits you.

items.name: Treating the skin helps the mind
items.note: When eczema treatment worked, people's anxiety and depression got better too.

items.name: Mind tools are backed by trials
items.note: Online CBT and mindfulness with self-compassion helped adults, including people who'd had eczema for about 27 years.

items.name: Small habits add up
items.note: Habit reversal on top of normal treatment helped the skin more than treatment alone.

items.name: "Not controlled" means it's time to step up
items.note: If treatment isn't working, the doctor can step it up. You haven't done anything wrong.

items.name: You're not alone
items.note: About 1 in 5 teens in South African cities report eczema symptoms.

items.name: Talking therapy
items.note: UK guidelines recommend it when eczema still affects daily life a lot, even with good skin treatment.

items.name: Mindfulness & self-compassion
items.note: An 8-week online course improved both quality of life and eczema in adults.

items.name: CBT (including online)
items.note: Helped with itch, stress, sleep problems and depression, and the benefits lasted a year.

items.name: Habit reversal
items.note: When the urge hits, press, pinch or clench your fists and count to 10 instead of scratching.

items.name: Relaxation and breathing
items.note: Helps stress more than skin, but it's low-risk and worth a try.

items.name: Managing ongoing stress and conflict
items.note: Stress and itch feed each other. Support from family or a counsellor helps break the cycle.

items.name: Say: "That looks itchy. Want the cold pack?"
items.note: You're offering help without blaming him.

items.name: Avoid: "Stop scratching!"
items.note: Scratching is often automatic. Being told off adds stress, and stress makes the itch worse.

items.name: Avoid: "Have you tried…?"
items.note: Remedies he didn't ask for get tiring. Rather ask, "Can I fetch anything from the pharmacy?"

items.name: Avoid: "It's just a rash" or "You'll grow out of it"
items.note: This plays down a lifelong condition. Try saying, "I know this is hard to live with."

items.name: Take one job off his plate
items.note: Reorder moisturiser, wash his bedding, keep spare tubs in the car, or put cream on his back (ask first).

items.name: Learn the emergency signs
items.note: Know what eczema herpeticum looks like (see Health) so he isn't the only one watching.

items.name: Spot a bad week
items.note: Bad sleep, cancelled plans, long sleeves in the heat, skipped treatment, or "what's the point". A gentle check-in helps.

items.name: Notice the wins
items.note: Say something when he has a calm night or sticks to his routine.

glossary.detail: A top everyday pick, for your skin or your general health. It doesn't mean a food or product cures eczema.
A habit or product that often makes eczema worse, like hot showers, bubble bath or fragrance.
Only used where histamine could really matter, mostly wine and beer, which can cause flushing and itch. "Histamine intolerance" diets haven't been shown to help eczema.
A cause that comes from inside the body (genes, skin barrier, immune system). Nobody did anything wrong.

glossary.meaning: The medical name for the most common type of eczema
glossary.detail: Long-term itchy, inflamed skin that comes and goes in flares. You can't catch it.

glossary.meaning: When eczema gets worse for a while
glossary.detail: Redder, itchier, sometimes weepy skin. When it settles down again, that's called remission.
Lotions, creams, gels and ointments that soften skin and repair the barrier. They're the base of all eczema care.

glossary.meaning: An emollient you wash with instead of soap
glossary.detail: Aqueous cream is fine for washing, but don't use it as a leave-on moisturiser.

glossary.meaning: Moisturise within about 3 minutes of bathing
glossary.detail: Pat dry, put medicine on the patches, then moisturiser everywhere else. This locks water into the skin.
The first choice for treating flares. Strengths go from mild (e.g. hydrocortisone 1%) to very potent. Safe when used as directed.
A line of cream from the tip of an adult's index finger to the first crease (about 0.5 g). Enough to cover two adult palms.
Once the skin has settled, steroid or tacrolimus cream goes on the usual flare spots twice a week to prevent new flares.
Very common, and it means flares often get under-treated. Used correctly, the benefits outweigh the risks.
Tacrolimus and pimecrolimus. Steroid-free creams that are good for the face, eyelids and folds.

glossary.meaning: An injected medicine that targets one part of the immune system
glossary.detail: For example dupilumab (Dupixent), tralokinumab, lebrikizumab and nemolizumab. Used for moderate–severe eczema.

glossary.meaning: A medicine that blocks inflammation signals inside cells
glossary.detail: Tablets (upadacitinib/Rinvoq, abrocitinib/Cibinqo, baricitinib) or creams (ruxolitinib). They work fast but need monitoring.

glossary.meaning: A damp cotton layer under a dry one
glossary.detail: Used for a short time on bad flares, with a doctor's guidance. Never on infected skin.
Can make moderate–severe eczema less severe, but only with a doctor's OK. The South African recipe is on the Water page.

glossary.meaning: A building block of the skin barrier
glossary.detail: Some people inherit weaker filaggrin, so water gets out and irritants get in.
Kids with eczema are more likely to get food allergy, asthma or hay fever, but many never do.
It grows easily on eczema skin and can cause infection. Look out for weeping, yellow crusts and pus spots.

glossary.meaning: Eczema infected with the cold-sore virus
glossary.detail: An emergency. Look out for painful clustered blisters, punched-out sores and fever. Get seen the same day.

glossary.meaning: Two different ways things make eczema worse
glossary.detail: Irritants (soap, wool, sweat) bother everyone's skin. Allergens (pollen, nickel, some foods) only affect people who are allergic to them.

glossary.meaning: A positive test doesn't always mean an allergy
glossary.detail: Skin-prick or blood tests can be positive without any real reaction. An oral food challenge is the most reliable test.
Not recommended unless an allergy is confirmed. It can lead to poor growth and new allergies.
Small amounts of allergens are taped to your back for a few days. Useful when creams, fabrics or metals seem to cause reactions.
Seven questions about the past week, scored 0–28. Families can fill it in at home to track eczema.
Used in clinics and trials to measure how much skin is affected and how badly.
Done at a dermatologist. Sunbathing and sunbeds aren't the same thing.
Notice the urge, then press, pinch or clench your fists for 30 seconds instead of scratching.

glossary.meaning: Darker or lighter patches after eczema
glossary.detail: Common on darker skin. They fade slowly once the eczema is under control.
